mainTopic: When a husband sells or gives a field to his wife: does she really own it, and does he still get to eat the פירות (the produce)?
overview: This amud discusses a husband who sells or gives a field to his wife. It opens with the end of a ruling that the wife owns a field she bought from him, but the husband eats its פירות. רבי אבא, רבי אבהו and the great sages of the generation say the 'sale' was really a gift, written as a sale to strengthen her rights. The גמרא challenges whether she owns it at all, from a ברייתא where a loan from one's wife or slave is treated as a trick to expose hidden money. It answers that a loan is different, because no one wants to be a 'servant to the lender'. רב rules that in a sale the husband eats the פירות, but in a gift he does not. רבי אלעזר, and רבי יוחנן as reported by רבין, say he does not eat them in either case, and רב חסדא ruled that way against the objection of רב's grandsons. רבא gives the הלכה, and the גמרא explains it with רב יהודה: if she paid with hidden money she does not acquire, but if her money was not hidden she does. The amud ends with a new ברייתא about not accepting deposits from women, slaves and children.

steps.title: End of the earlier ruling: the husband eats the produce
steps.stepSummary: The last words of a ruling from just before this section: the wife owns the field she bought from her husband, but the husband eats its פירות.
steps.whatsHappening: We are joining the end of a ruling that started just before this section. The ruling said that if a man sells a field to his wife, she owns it, and the husband still gets the produce while they are married.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two parts here. Ownership goes to the wife, but the right to the פירות stays with the בעל, as it does with other property a wife owns. The next step will offer a different reading of what the husband really meant.

keyTerms.meaning: Eats the produce, meaning he gets the profits or yield of the property

phrases.english: and the husband eats the produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes a ruling begun earlier on the daf.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wife who buys a field from her husband owns it, but the husband eats the פירות.

steps.title: The great sages: it was really a gift, written as a sale
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא, רבי אבהו and all the great sages of the generation say the husband really wanted to give the field as a gift. He only wrote 'sale' in the document to make her position stronger.
steps.simpleTranslation: However, רבי אבא, רבי אבהו and all the great sages of the generation said: He wanted to give it to her as a gift. So why did he write it as a sale? To strengthen her rights.
steps.whatsHappening: A group of great sages gives a different reading of the same case. In their view, the husband really meant to give his wife a gift, and the word 'sale' was only there to help her.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The word ברם signals a contrast with the earlier ruling. These sages look past the wording of the document to what the husband actually intended, which was a מתנה. A sale was seen as giving her a stronger hold on the field, so he used that wording for her benefit.

keyTerms.meaning: However; this introduces a contrasting view
The great sages of the generation
To strengthen her position or rights

steps.whyThisMatters: If it counts as a gift, the husband may lose his right to the פירות. Step 5 shows that רב treats a gift that way.

phrases.english: However, Rabbi Abba and Rabbi Abbahu
and all the great sages of the generation said:
He wanted to give it to her as a gift,
so why did he write it for her as a sale?
In order to strengthen her power.
phrases.notes: In other words, writing 'sale' was meant to give her a firmer hold on the field than the word 'gift' would.

steps.triggerLanguage: בְּרַם, רַבִּי אַבָּא וְרַבִּי אֲבָהוּ וְכׇל גְּדוֹלֵי הַדּוֹר אָמְרוּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a contrasting view of the same case: the 'sale' was really a gift.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A husband's 'sale' to his wife is really a gift, written as a sale to strengthen her rights.

steps.title: Challenge: a loan from a wife or slave is treated as a trick
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that if a man borrows from his slave and then frees him, or borrows from his wife and then divorces her, they cannot collect from him. The reason seems to be that the 'loan' was only a trick to bring hidden money into the open. So a 'sale' to his wife should also be a trick.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged this: If a man borrowed from his slave and then freed him, or borrowed from his wife and then divorced her, they have no claim against him. What is the reason? Is it not because we say he only wanted to expose the hidden money?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא to challenge the idea that the wife really owns the field she 'bought'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Money held by a slave or a wife was treated as belonging to the master or husband. So if they had money to lend him, it must have been hidden from him, and his 'loan' was a way to bring it out. If that logic applies here too, a 'sale' to his wife should also just be a trick to draw out her hidden money. Then she would not really acquire the field.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring hidden money into the open

phrases.english: They challenged: If he borrowed from the slave and freed him,
or from his wife and divorced her,
they have no claim against him at all.
What is the reason?
Is it not because we say:
he only wanted to expose the money?
phrases.notes: Literally 'to reveal coins.' The 'loan' was just a way to get them to show money they had hidden.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the idea that a wife truly acquires a field she 'bought' from her husband.
steps.kashyaTarget: The ruling that a wife acquires a field her husband sold to her.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If a loan from one's wife is treated as a trick to expose hidden money, a sale to her should be treated the same way, so she should not acquire.

steps.title: Answer: no one wants to be called a borrower
steps.stepSummary: A loan is different, because people dislike being 'a servant to the lender'. That makes it likely he never truly meant to borrow. A sale has no such shame, so it can be real.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is different there, because a person does not like to make himself 'the borrower is a servant to the lender'.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing why a loan is different from a sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Borrowing puts a person under the lender, as the פסוק in משלי says. So a man would not truly want to become his own slave's or wife's borrower, which means the loan was probably a trick. Selling a field carries no such shame, so we have no reason to think the sale was fake.

keyTerms.meaning: The borrower is a servant to the lender (משלי 22:7)

phrases.english: It is different there, for a person does not make himself
"the borrower is a servant to the lender."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge by pointing to a difference between a loan and a sale.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A sale to a wife should be a trick, just like a loan from her.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a loan is presumed fake, because people avoid being a borrower. A sale has no such reason, so it stands and the wife acquires.

steps.title: רב: sale versus gift and the husband's right to the produce
steps.stepSummary: רב rules that a field sold to a wife is hers, but the husband eats the פירות. A field given to her as a gift is hers, and the husband does not eat the פירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: One who sells a field to his wife, she acquires it, and the husband eats the produce. As a gift, she acquires it, and the husband does not eat the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a related ruling from רב that separates two cases: a sale and a gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In both cases the wife owns the field, so the difference is only about the פירות. When he gives it as a gift, he is understood to have given it to her completely, produce included. This also explains why step 2's 'it was really a gift' reading makes a difference.

phrases.english: Rav said: One who sells a field to his wife,
she has acquired it, and the husband eats the produce.
As a gift, she has acquired it,
and the husband does not eat the produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Brings a related ruling that separates a sale from a gift.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sale: the wife acquires and the husband eats the פירות. Gift: the wife acquires and the husband does not eat the פירות.

steps.title: רבי אלעזר: in both cases the husband gets no produce
steps.stepSummary: רבי אלעזר says that whether the field was sold or given, the wife acquires it and the husband does not eat the פירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי אלעזר said: Both in this case and in that case, she acquires it, and the husband does not eat the produce.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אלעזר disagrees with רב about the sale case and treats it just like a gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב and רבי אלעזר agree that the wife owns the field in both cases. They only disagree about a sale: רב gives the husband the פירות, while רבי אלעזר says the husband gets nothing in either case.

keyTerms.meaning: Both this and that; both cases are the same

steps.whatToRemember: רב and רבי אלעזר both agree that the wife acquires the field. They argue only about the פירות. רב says the husband keeps them in a sale, while רבי אלעזר says he does not keep them even in a sale. A loan from one's wife is different, and is treated as a trick to expose hidden money. Step 10 shows that רבא rules that in some sales she does not acquire at all.

phrases.english: And Rabbi Elazar said:
Both this and that, she has acquired it,
phrases.notes: 'This and that' means the sale case and the gift case from רב's ruling.

phrases.english: and the husband does not eat the produce.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר אָמַר: אֶחָד זֶה וְאֶחָד זֶה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב about the sale case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Whether sold or given, the wife acquires the field and the husband does not eat the פירות.

steps.title: רב חסדא rules in a real case like רבי אלעזר
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא decided an actual case following רבי אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב חסדא decided a real case following the view of רבי אלעזר.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא reports that רב חסדא ruled in a real case like רבי אלעזר: the wife owns the field, and the husband does not eat the פירות. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Two opinions were just quoted. רב said that in a sale the husband still eats the פירות, and רבי אלעזר said he does not. רב חסדא chose רבי אלעזר's side in practice, so the husband lost the פירות even in a sale.

keyTerms.meaning: An actual case; a ruling given in real life

phrases.english: Rav Chisda performed an action (ruled in a real case)
in accordance with Rabbi Elazar.

steps.triggerLanguage: עֲבַד רַב חִסְדָּא עוֹבָדָא כְּרַבִּי אֶלְעָזָר
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, the husband does not eat the פירות of a field he sold to his wife.

steps.title: רב's grandsons object: why follow the student over the teacher?
steps.stepSummary: רבן עוקבא and רבן נחמיה ask why רב חסדא left רב, the greater sage, and followed his student.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבן עוקבא and רבן נחמיה, the sons of רב's daughters, said to רב חסדא: Does the master leave the great sages and act like the lesser ones?!
steps.whatsHappening: רב's grandsons challenge רב חסדא's ruling. They ask why he followed a smaller sage instead of a greater one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רב was the great teacher, and רבי אלעזר was his student. Normally you follow the greater authority, so ruling against רב looks wrong.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַרוּ לֵיהּ רַבָּן עוּקְבָא וְרַבָּן נְחֶמְיָה
phrases.english: Rabban Ukva and Rabban Nechemya said to him
the sons of Rav's daughters, to Rav Chisda:
Does the master leave the great ones
phrases.notes: "The great one" here is רב, their grandfather.

phrases.english: and act like the lesser ones?!
phrases.notes: "The lesser one" is רבי אלעזר, who was רב's student.

steps.kashyaTarget: רב חסדא's choice to rule like רבי אלעזר against רב
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: You should follow the greater authority (רב), not his student.

steps.title: רב חסדא answers: רבי יוחנן agrees with me
steps.stepSummary: רב חסדא says he is also following a great sage, because רבין reported that רבי יוחנן holds like רבי אלעזר.
steps.simpleTranslation: He said to them: I too am acting like a great sage. When רבין came, he said in the name of רבי יוחנן: In both cases, sale and gift, she acquires the field, and the husband does not eat the פירות.
steps.whatsHappening: רב חסדא defends his ruling. He shows that a great sage, רבי יוחנן, holds the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The objection was "you followed a junior sage." רב חסדא answers that his view is not resting only on רבי אלעזר. רבי יוחנן, a top authority, says the same thing.

phrases.aramaic: אֲמַר לְהוּ: וַאֲנָא נָמֵי כְּרַבְרְבֵי עֲבַדִי,
phrases.english: He said to them: I too acted like the great ones,

phrases.aramaic: דְּכִי אֲתָא רָבִין אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: for when Ravin came, he said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
Both this and that, she has acquired,
phrases.notes: "This and that" means a sale and a gift.

phrases.english: and the husband does not eat the produce.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Brings a greater authority who supports the same view
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רב חסדא was relying only on a junior sage.
steps.terutzMaskana: He relies on רבי יוחנן, a great sage, who holds like רבי אלעזר.

steps.title: רבא gives the final הלכה on sale and gift
steps.stepSummary: רבא rules that in a sale she does not acquire and the husband eats the פירות, while in a gift she acquires and he does not eat the פירות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said, the הלכה is: If a man sells a field to his wife, she does not acquire it, and the husband eats the פירות. If he gives it as a gift, she acquires it, and the husband does not eat the פירות.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא states the practical הלכה for both cases: a sale and a gift.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For a gift, רבא agrees with רב: she acquires it and the husband does not eat the פירות. For a sale, he says 'she has not acquired', even though רב, רבי אלעזר and רבי יוחנן all said she acquires. That wording also sounds self-contradictory, and the גמרא questions it in step 11 and explains it in step 12.

phrases.english: Rava said, the halacha is:
One who sells a field to his wife, she has not acquired,
and the husband eats the produce.
With a gift, she has acquired,
and the husband does not eat the produce.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the final ruling. On a gift he agrees with רב. On a sale he departs from רב, רבי אלעזר and רבי יוחנן, who all said she acquires.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Sale: she does not acquire, and the husband eats the פירות. Gift: she acquires, and he does not eat the פירות.

steps.title: Two rulings that don't fit together?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks how רבא can say both "she did not acquire" and "the husband eats the פירות" in the sale case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Two?! (How can both parts of the sale ruling be true?)
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא points out a contradiction inside רבא's ruling about the sale.
steps.deeperAnalysis: "She did not acquire" means the field is still fully the husband's. But "the husband eats the פירות" suggests he only has the produce, which means the field itself is hers. Both cannot be true at once.
steps.confusionAlert: The problem is not sale versus gift. The problem is inside the sale ruling itself: "not hers" and "he only eats the פירות" clash.

phrases.english: Two?!
phrases.notes: He's asking: how can "she didn't acquire" and "he eats the פירות" both be true? If he only eats the פירות, the field sounds like hers.

steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If she did not acquire, the husband owns everything. Saying he "eats the פירות" implies she owns the field itself.

steps.title: Two different cases: hidden money vs. money in the open
steps.stepSummary: The two parts of the sale ruling describe two cases. If she paid with hidden money, she does not acquire. If her money was not hidden, she acquires and he eats the פירות. רב יהודה says the same.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is not difficult. Here it is about hidden money, and there it is about money that is not hidden. As רב יהודה said: with hidden money, she does not acquire; with money that is not hidden, she acquires.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the contradiction. רבא's two phrases are talking about two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If she paid with money she had hidden away, the sale was just a trick to bring that money out into the open, like the loan in step 3, so she does not acquire. If her money was known and not hidden, the sale is real. She owns the field, but the husband eats the פירות. רב יהודה's statement backs this split.
steps.whatToRemember: A sale to a wife paid with hidden money is not real, so she does not acquire. Paid with money that is not hidden, she acquires the field, and the husband still eats the פירות. A gift is fully hers, without פירות for him.

phrases.english: It is not difficult;
here, with hidden money,
phrases.notes: Money she had hidden away. The "sale" was just a way to bring it into the open.

phrases.english: there, with money that is not hidden –
as Rav Yehuda said:
Hidden money, she has not acquired,
money that is not hidden, she has acquired.

steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the ruling into two different cases
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Both phrases describe one single case, which would be a contradiction.
steps.terutzMaskana: Hidden money: no acquisition. Money that is not hidden: she acquires, and he eats the פירות.

steps.title: New topic: deposits from women, slaves and children
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא teaches that one should not accept פקדונות from women, slaves or children. If he did accept one, he returns it to them, and if they died, to the husband or master.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: We do not accept deposits from women, slaves or children. If he accepted from a woman, he returns it to the woman, and if she died, he returns it to her husband. If he accepted from a slave, he returns it to the slave, and if he died, he returns it to his master.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new related topic with a ברייתא about accepting deposits from people who usually don't own property.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Women, slaves and children usually do not have their own property, so the item may really belong to the husband, master or parent. That is why one should not accept such deposits to begin with. But once accepted, he returns it to the person who gave it, since it might truly be theirs. After death it goes to the husband or master.
steps.whyThisMatters: This continues the theme of whether a wife (or slave) can really own property apart from her husband (or master).

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
We do not accept deposits –

phrases.aramaic: לֹא מִן הַנָּשִׁים, וְלֹא מִן הָעֲבָדִים,
phrases.english: not from women, and not from slaves,
and not from children.
If he accepted from a woman, he returns it to the woman,
and if she died, he returns it to her husband.
If he accepted from a slave, he returns it to the slave,
and if he died, he returns it to his master.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new related topic about property held by a wife or slave.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Do not accept deposits from women, slaves or children. If accepted, return it to the giver, or after death to the husband or master.
